title: Porous surfaces and unsalvageable materials
audience: Coordinators, supervisors and trained workers who may triage, refer, document or support biohazard and trauma-related work. This lesson does not grant authority to enter, assess, clean, decontaminate, release, transport or dispose of anything in a regulated setting.
learningOutcomes: Explain why porous materials can hold contamination that is not visible.
Hold a porous item out of use until a specialist decision is recorded.
Record property, risk and disposal decisions as three separate entries.

instruction.heading: Porous materials and disposal decisions
instruction.body: Soft furnishings, underlays, timber joints and similar porous materials can keep contamination that cannot be seen on the surface. Decisions to keep, remove or dispose of such material must be made by a competent, authorised person and must follow the property, insurance and waste controls that apply. A proposed treatment for a potentially contaminated item, such as a mattress, needs specialist review first, because a method that moves material or changes the contamination can make things worse. Keep three questions apart in the decision memo: the preservation of property, the risk evaluation and the authorisation for specialist disposal. Do not prescribe intrusive treatment of unknown contamination.

procedure: Identify the material and whether it is porous, concealed or hard to reach.
Do not treat the item until a specialist has assessed it.
Record the property owner's position and the insurer's position as separate entries.
Record the risk evaluation as its own entry.
Record the disposal authorisation as its own entry, naming who approved it.
Keep the item out of use and out of shared areas until the decision is made.

workedExamples.situation: A cleaner proposes to wash a soiled mattress on site to save it.
workedExamples.reasoning: No. The mattress is porous and may carry concealed contamination, and washing on site may move it. The mattress stays out of use and goes to specialist review.

workedExamples.situation: An owner asks for a carpet to be kept because it looks clean.
workedExamples.reasoning: Not yet. Looking clean is not evidence. The carpet waits for the specialist decision, and the insurer position is recorded in its own entry.

equipmentAndPpe: PPE for handling as set by the assessment. Porous items are not handled without the plan.
Sealed and labelled containers as the plan specifies.

commonErrors.error: Keeping porous items because they look clean.
commonErrors.prevention: Keep them out of use until the specialist decides.

commonErrors.error: Washing or treating an item on site without review.
commonErrors.prevention: Send it for specialist review first.

commonErrors.error: Mixing property, risk and disposal decisions in one note.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Decisions on retention or disposal are restricted to competent, authorised people under the applicable rules. Completing this lesson gives no authority to make them.
Disposal of contaminated material must follow the waste rules of the state or territory where the work is done. Check those rules first.
Insurance and property decisions are separate from health and safety decisions.

qualityStandard: Every porous item has a specialist decision recorded before any treatment or disposal.
The three questions appear as separate entries in the memo.
documentationEvidence: Decision memo with three separate entries.
Item register showing each item's status.
summary: Porous material can hold what cannot be seen.
Keep property, risk and disposal decisions apart.

knowledgeChecks.question: A cleaner proposes to wash a contaminated mattress on site. What is correct?
options: Wash it, because it saves the client money.
Wash it and record the result.
Hold it out of use and send it for specialist review first.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why keep property, risk and disposal decisions separate?
options: Because each needs its own authority and evidence, and mixing them hides gaps.
Because they are paid for by different people.
Because the form requires three signatures.

officialReferences.title: Duties of a person conducting a business or undertaking (PCBU)
officialReferences.covers: Read via WebFetch on 2026-11-03. The PCBU must protect workers and others so far as reasonably practicable; hazards are eliminated where possible and otherwise minimised; for certain hazards a hierarchy of control applies (the page does not list its levels); duties cannot be contracted out. The page does not cover trauma cleaning, waste or PPE rules. Publisher: Safe Work Australia. The state or territory regulator confirms the adopted law.

officialReferences.title: Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare (2019)
officialReferences.covers: Read via WebFetch on 2026-11-03, first 100,000 of 133,773 characters only. Read: section 2.2 (standard precautions apply to all people), section 3.1.2 recommendations 7 and 8 (sharps handled minimally, never recapped, bent or broken, disposed of at point of use in an approved container not filled past its maximum fill line), section 3.1.3 recommendation 12 (spill response with gloves and protective equipment, containment, absorbent removal, detergent cleaning). Healthcare-setting guidance, applied here by analogy. Publisher: National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC).

officialReferences.title: Managing spills of blood and body fluids and substances
officialReferences.covers: Read via WebFetch on 2026-11-03. Standard precautions and PPE for all spill cleaning; clear up the spill before cleaning the area and do not add liquid to a spill; avoid aerosols; leak-proof bags and containers for waste; sodium hypochlorite generally unnecessary for spill management. Victorian guidance only.

officialReferences.title: Managing exposures to blood and body fluids or substances
officialReferences.covers: Read via WebFetch on 2026-11-03. First response: remove contaminated clothing, wash with soap and water, flush mucous membranes, rinse eyes gently, report immediately; remove from duty and carry out a risk assessment; medical evaluation with post-exposure prophylaxis where appropriate; document date, time, type and circumstances. Victorian guidance only. The page shows its last update as 2015.

officialReferences.title: Cleaning and waste disposal procedures for infection control
officialReferences.covers: Read via WebFetch on 2026-11-03. Three waste groups (general, clinical, pharmaceutical); clinical waste in biohazard bags shown as yellow; sharps into containers that meet the Australian and New Zealand standards named on the page; clinical and pharmaceutical waste collected by waste companies licensed by the EPA and taken to EPA-licensed facilities. Victorian guidance only.

moduleAuthority.heading: Module authority and restricted work
moduleAuthority.body: This module is training content. It does not grant authority to enter, assess, clean, decontaminate, release, transport or dispose of anything at a scene or in any regulated setting. Completing this lesson does not give a licence, certificate, clearance or permission to do restricted work. Some of the work described here is restricted to licensed, authorised or specially trained people, and some of it may not be done by a general cleaner at all. Where legal, police, coronial, insurer, property-owner or occupational-health authority applies, that authority must be obtained and recorded before any step is taken. Nothing in this lesson replaces the employer's written procedure, the site-specific assessment or the decision of the competent, authorised party. Where you cannot identify who holds that authority, the answer is to stop and refer.

stopWorkAndReferral.heading: Stop-work and referral rules for this module
stopWorkAndReferral.body: Stop work and refer whenever any of the following is true: the biological hazard is uncertain or the contamination status is unverified; the required authorisation, release or competence is missing; the handling, transport, waste or exposure protocol is unknown; a sharp has been found or might be present; a worker may have been exposed; entry has been offered without written release; a party asks you to certify clearance or unrestricted re-entry. A stop-work decision is not a failure. Restart only after the authorised supervisor has documented the procedure and a qualified review has been completed.
